evidence.claim: Articles 72-75 make the Prime Minister the Cabinet's representative who submits bills, reports on foreign relations, and exercises control and supervision over administrative branches; the Cabinet conducts foreign affairs, concludes treaties with Diet approval, prepares the budget, and laws and cabinet orders are signed by the competent minister and countersigned by the Prime Minister.
evidence.title: The Constitution of Japan
evidence.excerpt: Articles 72-75 make the Prime Minister the Cabinet's representative who submits bills, reports on foreign relations, and exercises control and supervision over administrative branches; the Cabinet conducts foreign affairs, concludes treaties with Diet approval, prepares the budget, and laws and cabinet orders are signed by the competent minister and countersigned by the Prime Minister.
evidence.source_confidence_reason: Authoritative constitutional text from the official legal translation site; stable baseline for office powers.
evidence.ruler_attribution: Defines Kishida's office-level authority and constraints rather than a ruler-specific act.
contrary_evidence: Text does not show informal coalition limits or day-to-day bargaining constraints.

evidence.claim: Kishida tied women's economic independence, anti-violence measures, loneliness support, fertility treatment coverage, the Children and Families Agency, and disability support to his new capitalism agenda.
evidence.title: Policy Speech by Prime Minister KISHIDA Fumio to the 208th Session of the Diet
evidence.excerpt: Kishida tied women's economic independence, anti-violence measures, loneliness support, fertility treatment coverage, the Children and Families Agency, and disability support to his new capitalism agenda.
evidence.source_confidence_reason: Primary PMO transcript with direct policy commitments and institutional design language.
evidence.ruler_attribution: Direct Kishida agenda-setting; downstream effects depend on legislation, ministries, and budgets.
contrary_evidence: This is a policy vision and not a measured outcome; high inherited Japanese welfare levels limit how much marginal improvement can be inferred from rhetoric alone.

evidence.claim: The June 2022 revised Child Welfare Act responded to child abuse and isolated caregiving conditions by adding municipal comprehensive support, child-family centers, and a certified qualification in child-welfare practice.
evidence.title: 令和4年6月に成立した改正児童福祉法について
evidence.excerpt: The June 2022 revised Child Welfare Act responded to child abuse and isolated caregiving conditions by adding municipal comprehensive support, child-family centers, and a certified qualification in child-welfare practice.
evidence.source_locator: official page summary / search snippet describing the 2022 revision
evidence.source_confidence_reason: Official government summary of a 2022 law; the page is later but the law and policy change are clearly described.
evidence.period_fit: 2022 law and 2022 policy context; later webpage summarizes the change
evidence.ruler_attribution: Kishida cabinet legislative agenda with municipal implementation; outcomes remain partly downstream.
contrary_evidence: This shows institutional reform, not direct proof that abuse or isolation fell in 2022.

evidence.claim: Kishida said women's economic independence was central to the new form of capitalism, that Japan would close the gender wage gap by mandatory disclosure, promote post-delivery paternity leave, and provide temporary shelters for women fleeing Afghanistan and Ukraine.
evidence.title: Opening Remarks by Prime Minister KISHIDA Fumio at the World Assembly for Women: WAW! 2022
evidence.excerpt: Kishida said women's economic independence was central to the new form of capitalism, that Japan would close the gender wage gap by mandatory disclosure, promote post-delivery paternity leave, and provide temporary shelters for women fleeing Afghanistan and Ukraine.
evidence.source_confidence_reason: Primary PMO transcript with direct gender-equality and vulnerable-group commitments.
evidence.ruler_attribution: Direct Kishida policy framing and external-aid commitment; implementation involved multiple ministries and partners.
contrary_evidence: These are commitments and aid examples, not a direct measure of women’s lived outcomes in 2022.

evidence.claim: Kishida said the government would provide average households with 47,000 yen of assistance, give 100,000 yen in support to pregnant women and families raising children without income caps, raise the childbirth lump-sum allowance to 500,000 yen, and keep children at the center of policy.
evidence.title: Press Conference by Prime Minister Kishida
evidence.excerpt: Kishida said the government would provide average households with 47,000 yen of assistance, give 100,000 yen in support to pregnant women and families raising children without income caps, raise the childbirth lump-sum allowance to 500,000 yen, and keep children at the center of policy.
evidence.source_confidence_reason: Primary PMO transcript with concrete, quantified support measures and explicit universality language.
evidence.ruler_attribution: Direct Kishida cabinet budget and family-policy announcement; execution depended on the Diet and administrative agencies.
contrary_evidence: The package was announced during high inflation, so some relief may only offset losses rather than create net welfare gains.

evidence.claim: Kishida said the supplementary budget would put 1 trillion yen over five years into people through reskilling, career changes, and transitions to permanent employment, and that his task force would check the progress of all budget measures every week.
evidence.title: Press Conference by Prime Minister Kishida
evidence.excerpt: Kishida said the supplementary budget would put 1 trillion yen over five years into people through reskilling, career changes, and transitions to permanent employment, and that his task force would check the progress of all budget measures every week.
evidence.source_confidence_reason: Primary PMO transcript; the monitoring mechanism and workforce-investment scale are explicit.
evidence.ruler_attribution: Direct Kishida cabinet management choice; actual take-up and labor-market effects depended on firms, workers, and ministries.
contrary_evidence: This is strong on monitoring and planned investment, but weak on verified end-year welfare outcomes.

evidence.claim: Japan's latest 2022 child-related SDG figures show near-universal water and sanitation access, 99 percent DTP3 coverage, 98 percent MCV1 coverage, and very low maternal and under-five mortality.
evidence.title: Child-Related SDG Progress Assessment for Japan
evidence.excerpt: Japan's latest 2022 child-related SDG figures show near-universal water and sanitation access, 99 percent DTP3 coverage, 98 percent MCV1 coverage, and very low maternal and under-five mortality.
evidence.source_locator: dashboard rows for water, sanitation, immunization, and mortality indicators
evidence.source_confidence_reason: Official UNICEF dashboard using international agency data; strong for country-level outcome context, though not ruler-specific.
evidence.period_fit: latest available year 2022, useful baseline context for the target year
evidence.ruler_attribution: Country-level baseline only; does not isolate Kishida's marginal contribution.
contrary_evidence: High national averages can hide subgroup gaps, and the dashboard does not attribute changes to the prime minister.

evidence.claim: OECD reported that Japan remained among the highest-performing systems in PISA 2022, with improved student belonging since 2018, but still experienced long COVID-related school closures for 16 percent of students and weekly remote-learning difficulties for some students.
evidence.title: PISA 2022 Results (Volume I and II) - Country Notes: Japan
evidence.excerpt: OECD reported that Japan remained among the highest-performing systems in PISA 2022, with improved student belonging since 2018, but still experienced long COVID-related school closures for 16 percent of students and weekly remote-learning difficulties for some students.
evidence.source_locator: country note sections on performance, school life, and learning during COVID-related school closures
evidence.source_confidence_reason: Official OECD country note with standard PISA methodology and clear 2022 Japan indicators.
evidence.period_fit: 2022 educational outcomes and disruptions, published after the test but directly about the target period
evidence.ruler_attribution: Country-system context only; useful for baseline and crisis-education effects, not direct prime-minister attribution.
contrary_evidence: The note does not isolate Kishida's specific causal impact, and much of the educational baseline long predates 2022.

evidence.claim: OECD's basic-statistics table for Japan reported a 15.7 percent relative poverty rate, 9.9 percent female share of parliament, 2.6 percent of GNI spent on education, and 11.5 percent spent on health care.
evidence.title: Basic statistics of Japan, 2022: OECD Economic Surveys: Japan 2024
evidence.excerpt: OECD's basic-statistics table for Japan reported a 15.7 percent relative poverty rate, 9.9 percent female share of parliament, 2.6 percent of GNI spent on education, and 11.5 percent spent on health care.
evidence.source_locator: society / public and private spending rows in the basic statistics table
evidence.source_confidence_reason: Official OECD table compiled from recognized international datasets; strong for baseline and residual-gap context.
evidence.period_fit: published after the target year but reporting baseline context from 2018-2021 alongside 2022 survey framing
evidence.ruler_attribution: Country-level baseline and inherited constraints only; not direct evidence of Kishida-specific change.
contrary_evidence: The table mostly reflects inherited structural conditions and does not prove 2022 ruler-specific improvement or deterioration.

unresolved_gaps: Stronger direct evidence of Kishida's personal control over police, prosecutors, and protective institutions before and after the Abe assassination.
More evidence that the church-scandal and protest responses reduced actual harm rather than only improving the public narrative.
More independent evidence that the 2022 growth/distribution package actually changed household welfare or investment outcomes rather than only announcing them.
Better separation of Kishida's policy effect from BOJ policy, exchange-rate moves, and imported inflation shocks.
Direct year-end outcome evidence for child, fertility, and social-service gains attributable to the 2022 package.
More subgroup evidence on single-parent households, disabled people, housing insecurity, and food insecurity.
Direct, traceable evidence of Kishida's own assets, private interests, donor links, or personal self-enrichment is missing.
Independent corroboration of the personal claim that Kishida had no links to the former Unification Church and that his vetting instructions were fully followed.
More independent evidence on whether the 2022 startup, digital, and green-growth agenda actually produced measurable execution, not just planning.
Clearer separation of Kishida's own execution from external shocks and inherited macro conditions when judging the economic package and wage trajectory.
